books.section: The United States as an Imperialist Power

stimulus.source_note: Louis Dalrymple, "School Begins," Puck magazine, January 25, 1899; Library of Congress cph.3b48925; public domain.
stimulus.text: Louis Dalrymple, "School Begins," Puck magazine, January 25, 1899. Uncle Sam, a white-haired teacher with glasses and a goatee, leans over a desk holding a long pointer. Four small children sit on a bench in front of him, wearing sashes labeled Philippines, Hawaii, Porto Rico, and Cuba. Behind them, older children sit at desks reading books labeled California, Texas, Arizona, and New Mexico. A blackboard reads: "The U.S. must govern its new territories with or without their consent until they can govern themselves." The cartoon was printed with this caption: "Uncle Sam (to his new class in Civilization)—Now, children, you've got to learn these lessons whether you want to or not! But just take a look at the class ahead of you, and remember that, in a little while, you will feel as glad to be here as they are!"

source: original; stimulus is a public-domain 1899 political cartoon by Louis Dalrymple, Puck magazine
stem: The blackboard says the United States "must govern its new territories with or without their consent until they can govern themselves." That line shows the cartoonist believes

options.text: The territories asked to be governed
options.misconception: The caption says the children must learn whether they want to or not; nobody asked for the lessons.

options.text: Empire requires ruling peoples who did not choose American rule

options.misconception: Congress did the opposite: it ratified the Treaty of Paris and kept the Philippines.

options.text: The Philippines had already become a state of the Union
options.misconception: The Philippines never became a state; the cartoon shows it as a child still needing lessons.

rationales.A: The caption says the children must learn whether they want to or not. Consent is not part of the picture.
rationales.B: The blackboard is blunt: govern them with or without their consent, until they can govern themselves.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the Senate ratified the Treaty of Paris in February 1899, keeping the Philippines.
rationales.D: The Philippines sits on the front bench as a pupil, not a state. It stayed a colony until 1946.
rationales.general:
1. Read the blackboard. The United States must govern its new territories with or without their consent.
2. Read the caption. The children must learn whether they want to or not.
3. Name the idea. Empire here means ruling peoples who never chose American rule.
Remember: when a cartoon states its argument in writing, quote the writing, because the drawing alone can mislead.
